subsubtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EXCISE TAX ON CANADIAN WINES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing importance.
Given the announcement this morning that double-digit inflation has hit the consumers of Canada for the first time since a former Liberal government imposed wage and price controls in 1975, after saying they could never do so, given that a substantial portion of this increase flows directly from the excise taxes introduced by the present Minister of Finance on April 21 last, and given the fact that much of this stems from the imposition of the excise tax on Canadian wines, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz):
That this government begin its fight against inflation by removing the excise tax imposed on Canadian wines as contained within the mini-budget of the Minister of Finance introduced last April 21.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the United States is responsible for the majority portion of acid rain which affects Canada, and is currently planning a massive expansion of coal-based facilities without adequate pollution control equipment, and in view of the American refusal to enter into meaningful negotiations or agreements with Canada on this crucial health, environment and economic question, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this House record its disgust with the Prime Minister and his supine cabinet for their continuing and ongoing sell-out of Canada to the United States on every major issue, including acid rain; and, further, that this House records the shame of a Liberal policy which promotes the sale of clean, non-polluting Canadian energy to the U.S. when they are daily responding with an attitude and policies that pollute and destroy the Canadian environment and health.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my motion is also under Standing Order 43 and it ties in with the motion presented by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan).
Having regard to the fact that the government has given recognition to the severe financial hardships which are suffered by people who live in northern and isolated areas of our country, and is therefore maintaining a very elaborate system through which employees of the federal government are compensated through northern living and isolation allowances, and having regard to the fact that the government has recently made the necessary changes to the Income Tax Act to provide for these allowances to be earned free of taxes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
July 18, 1980

That the Minister of Finance give serious consideration, in the course of preparing himself for a budget, to the establishment of a more permanent and universal system which would afford all taxpayers who live remote from the mainstream of life in Canada, which flows in a narrow corridor along the U.S. border, treatment under the Income Tax Act which would be to a degree more equitable and fair and in accordance with their ability to pay.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.

Belanger Limitee, of Montmagny, Quebec, made an application-which was subsequently withdrawn in 1972-but closed down its subsidiary in Carleton Place, some 35 miles from here, costing some 220 jobs there, and in view of the fact that the federal government, with the provincial government, gave almost $2 million to A. Belanger Limitee in 1974-1975, and now that that company is owned by Admiral Corporation it is taking a further 270 jobs from Ottawa, is it the minister's view that losing 500 jobs in the Ottawa Valley through DREE grants to one company, namely, Belanger, making home appliances in Montmagny, is fair and reasonable for the Ottawa Valley?

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF DREE GRANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the minister responsible for DREE and is a follow-up to the question which was asked by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton.
Is the minister aware that there are a great many other industries in provinces which are not favoured by DREE, communities which are suffering the same disaster with industries going to more attractive parts of the country where the DREE program applies? When one province receives 43 per cent of all DREE grants there is a strong inducement for industries to leave one province to go to the province where they can qualify for a DREE grant. I find this throughout central Ontario with industries employing up to probably 200 or 300 people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre De Bane (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF DREE GRANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my philosophy is essentially that we should try to build on the potential of each region. I, personally, do not think that we can play one region against the other.
If the hon. member is interested, I would be very agreeable to giving him all of the different figures for every region. He thinks his is not receiving enough. I am very pleased to say to the hon. member that I discussed this particular riding with several Ontario ministers of the provincial government to see to what extent both levels of government, and particularly through my department, can do something for his riding. However, I do not think we should criticize what we are doing in every region, because I think that would be quite counterproductive.
I could give examples. Just to give one, recently the province of Quebec asked me for a grant to build an industry in the poorest region of the province of Quebec, the Magdalen Islands. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MR. ARTHUR STANLEY SILVERMAN AS ADMINISTRATOR
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that in April, 1979, my predecessor, after consultation with the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services, invited the Auditor General to undertake a thorough review of the House of Commons administration. You will also recall that in October, 1979, the results of the preliminary investigation made by the Auditor General on the administration of the House of Commons were delivered to Mr. Jerome with a number of key recommendations under the form of an interim report. My predecessor immediately responded to that recommendation and accepted the proposal of the Auditor General to appoint Mr. Rheal Chatelain, senior deputy Auditor General, as acting administrator of the House of Commons. Mr. Chatelain took up his duties here at the end of November, 1979.

The dissolution of the House of Commons delayed the early consideration of the Auditor General's interim report, but 1 have now had an opportunity to discuss his principal recommendations with the commissioners of internal economy and with members of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services. I thank them for their assistance to me in this very important and complex matter.
1 want to say to the House that, after giving very careful consideration to the various aspects of the administrative structure of the House of Commons, I have concluded that the Speaker and the House must be supported by a professional administrative staff to provide the services and systems necessary. Therefore, I have taken the necessary steps to create the position of administrator, whose authority will derive from the Speaker, and after careful consideration of the qualifications and experience of a number of candidates I have appointed Mr. Arthur Stanley Silverman to that position. Mr. Silverman is a certified general accountant with 15 years' experience in private industry and in government. He comes to us well qualified and very highly recommended, and I am sure that hon. members will give him every assistance as he assumes the important responsibilities of his new office.

subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES-NORTHERN PIPELINE ACT-USE OF ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the matter of privilege which 1 wish to raise arises out of this morning's question period, in particular the answer which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave to the leader of this party, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). I should like to say that I think this point of privilege touches one of the most important issues in the operation of Parliament, namely, the relationship between the executive and Parliament. This relationship shows up most prominently in the instances where the government uses its order in council power.
What we have before us at the present time is an example of the use of that power by the government under the Northern Pipeline Act in a way which some of us think is questionable. Let me say immediately that I recognize there is a debatable point, but the difficulty is that if the government has used an order in council authority which does not exist and goes ahead with the construction of the pre-build of the northern pipeline, it will soon be the case that it will be too late for Parliament to exercise its authority.
I recognize, Your Honour, that all regulations and orders passed by the government are referred in due course to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, and I assume, therefore, that this order in council will eventually get into the hands of that committee. But if the House were to adjourn soon, there is no telling when that consideration might be given. In other words, the construction of the line could be undertaken before anybody has had the opportunity to consider the question as to whether or not it is legal.
1 remind Your Honour that there have been occasions when orders in council passed by the government, which the government claimed were legal, proved to be otherwise. 1 have in mind, in particular, an order in council passed by the Diefen-baker government in 1962 having to do with the increasing of import duties and certain other taxes. I will not take the time to tell the House the story of that incident, but the matter was taken to court and, as a result of its being taken to court, the Liberal government which followed a year later found it necessary to introduce a statute to legalize what had been done by the Diefenbaker government under an order in council.
I am prepared to admit that the question of whether it was legal or illegal never was settled; the Liberal government took no chance on the courts deciding against the order in council because, if that had happened, the amounts of money to be paid back would have been tremendous. But the fact that the government of that day did act as it did suggests that it certainly had doubts about the legality of that order in council.
I say that this situation confronts us now. I know the arguments that are made both ways. We contend that the Northern Pipeline Act provides-and the definition is very clear-for the building of one pipeline from Alaska across
Privilege-Mr. Knowles
Canada into the lower 48 states. We contend that the building of only a portion of that line is not consistent with the provisions of the act. In fact, we contend that what was intended to be a transportation medium for American gas to move from Alaska to the rest of the United States has been turned into an export pipeline for the purpose of exporting Canadian gas to the United States.
The government's argument, on the other hand, is that it has authority under section 20(4) of the act to amend the terms of condition 12 in schedule III. 1 do not agree but I am prepared to admit that there are arguments on both sides. But my point of privilege, Madam Speaker, is this, that unless something is done now, it can be too late. Perhaps down the road somewhere the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments will find that the order in council exceeded the authority set out in the act or that there should be court action about it, and by that time, of course, the construction could be under way and it would be a very costly proposition to alter it or change it at that time.
I feel therefore, Madam Speaker, that the time to get this matter settled is now, before the pipeline is started rather than afterward. I shall indicate what I suggest. I suggest that the matter should be referred to a standing committee of the House. If you find, either today or on Monday, that I have a prima facie case of privilege, I would be prepared to move such a motion. The usual motion when one raises a point of privilege is to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, but because this order in council would eventually go to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, 1 think it might be appropriate for the motion to read that it be referred forthwith to that committee so that it can investigate it right away.
As I say, Madam Speaker, this touches on a pretty important matter in our parliamentary relations. There is no doubt about our position and that we have views about the pre-build; I do not deny that for a moment. But I am speaking now as one who is concerned about how government and Parliament operate and I just do not buy the idea of government arguing by assertion, saying that it has the right to do under section 20(4) of the Northern Pipeline Act what it has done. I just do not buy the argument that the government has the right to say that a bill which provided for a transportation link between Alaska and the lower 48 states can now be turned into authority to build a southern Alberta pipeline for the export of Canadian gas to the United States.
I submit, Your Honour, that Parliament has the right to have this legal question at least reviewed by some body responsible to us, and I hope that you will give the matter serious consideration.
The Prime Minister suggested today to the leader of this party that he would accept an amendment which we might move to the adjournment motion. I would remind the Prime Minister that you, Your Honour, are the one to decide on whether an amendment is acceptable, I can also tell him and I can tell you that since that suggestion was made I have tried to

July 18, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Knowles
draft one; 1 have one ready for the hon. member for Oshawa when he speaks later. 1 can see procedural problems about it, but in no case can we draft an amendment to a motion to adjourn the House for a recess in such a way that it gives the government the authority to act by order in council with respect to a matter that is spelled out so clearly in a statute of Parliament.
1 hope that this amendment which I have drafted will be accepted and we can have a debate on it and vote on it at some time, Monday, Tuesday or whenever we get around to it. But in the meantime it seems to me the basic question of the right of the executive to say to itself that it can do this under the terms of the act must be reviewed.
I go back to an incident which I hope will not annoy my Conservative friends because I am referring to something that happened in their time; it is just the one that comes to my mind. I recall so well how, on the floor of this House in 1962, we challenged the then prime minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, to get a court consideration of the matter. He just stood up and said, with all the power of assertion the late right honourable gentleman had, that it was in order, that the government had the authority to use two statutes-one was the Customs Tariff and the other was the Financial Administration Act-to raise duties considerably on the one hand and then forgive them and put them back a little on the other. In fact, however, changing the rates of duty cannot be done by a government unless it has the authority of Parliament.
I am making the point that this sort of thing has been done. Just because the prime minister, whether it was Mr. Diefenbaker or the present one, stood up and said, "What we are doing is within order in council powers", does not make it such.
When the Hon. John Turner was minister of justice, the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments was set up. It is a very important committee. The government argued then that the power of regulation or the power to do things by order in council had to be put within certain limits. One of the limits he proposed, which supposedly would protect the rights of Parliament under this, was this standing joint committee to which all orders and regulations would stand referred. That committee has been a joint committee of both Houses. It has had opposition persons, at least from our side, in the chair of the committee. It has done some awfully good work, and I would be quite happy to accept the judgment of that joint committee on this. But there is not much point in getting that judgment some time after October 15, which is the date that it is proposed we come back.
I present this matter to Madam Speaker as a very serious question of privilege. I do not deny my bias and the bias of my party in so far as the policy is concerned, but I ask Your Honour to join with me in looking beyond that to the importance of an action by the government which, in my view, transcends its authority to act by order in council under a statute. One of the basic principles around here is just thatyes, governments can pass orders in council but only if they are given that authority.
I well remember back in the days of World War II that we used to be astounded by the things the government could pass by order in council. It was able to do so because of the War Measures Act under which it could do anything. I remember we came down here in November, 1944, for a special week's session to deal with the conscription crisis. At that point the pay of members of Parliament was only $4,000 a year, and we had had our $4,000. Most of the members who had come for that week in November were finding it pretty difficult to get enough dollars together on which to live, but the government solved the problem by using the War Measures Act to pass an order in council giving us $25 a day for seven days. As I say, the War Measures Act was all pervasive; the government could do anything under it. But once that is no longer there, no order in council can be passed by the government unless there is authority for it in a statute.
Now, the Prime Minister said that the government have the authority under section 20(4) of the Northern Pipeline Act. We question that. Their argument may prevail over ours if it gets before a proper court, but I deny the right of the government simply to stand up and argue by assertion that they have the right and therefore Parliament just has to take it.
Therefore, I raise this matter as a serious question of privilege. If Your Honour Finds either now or after you have reflected on it that I have a prima facie case, I would be pleased to move that the matter be referred to whichever committee Your Honour advises, either to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections or to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES-NORTHERN PIPELINE ACT-USE OF ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has couched this as a question of privilege. I do not know whether it is a question of privilege in the sense that Your Honour has defined it, but I think whether or not it is a question of privilege is academic at this point.
The hon. member has really said that he takes the view that orders in council or other instruments which have been issued, promulgated, passed or whatever by the government, are passed without authority in the statute. It is a matter of elementary parliamentary law and elementary law that there must be power in the statute before such orders can be passed.
The minister has not yet tabled the documents respecting other matters which he undertook to do today. But if that is the issue in terms of the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, then I think whether or not it is a question of privilege the issue regarding the power to pass that order in council can be settled, and I respectfully suggest should be settled, at least in the parliamentary sense.
Of course, the place for the settlement of that issue is in the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments; I think that would be the appropriate one. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to possibly
July 18, 1980

two committees, but I think that is the appropriate committee. It is important that the issue be settled, at least in so far as we can settle it here in Parliament from the points of view of the government on the one hand, and members of Parliament on the other, respecting the relationship of the executive to Parliament and, of course, respecting the producers and users of the facility which is the subject of the argument and was the subject of the statement last night by the minister.
Our hope is to facilitate the early settlement of that point in so far as Parliament may be able to settle it. From our party's point of view, we would be prepared to consent to a reference now of that matter to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, that that reference take place, that the committee convene quickly next week whether or not Parliament is sitting, and that the issue which has been placed squarely by the member go to committee so that in a parliamentary sense it can be settled and dealt with.
In my judgment and in my respectful submission, that does not take away any other rights that are there. Let me be clear about that. It does not take away the right of a citizen to go to court. Whether that citizen is a member of Parliament or otherwise, he has that right. But at least it would settle that issue.
If we could agree upon that today, then I think the business of the House could proceed and at least there would be some certainty put on the question of the legality or illegality of what the government has done. I am not passing any judgment on that because I have not seen the documents; they are to be tabled later on today, according to the undertaking of the minister. At least it would settle the question that has been put squarely and was the subject of a considerable amount of debate last night.
I just want to make it clear that we would be prepared to consent to that kind of arrangement and to negotiate that kind of an arrangement if that were the case, because I think it is important that it be settled.
[ Translation}

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES-NORTHERN PIPELINE ACT-USE OF ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with all due respect to the experience of the hon. member who rose on what he called a question of privilege, I must unfortunately differ from him with regard to the substance of his intervention. Basically he claims that the order approved by the governor in council should be subject to examination by this Parliament, or a committee of the House, before being applied; that is to say, he would like the order in council authorizing the construction of the pre-build, as an integral part of the whole pipeline, to be studied by Parliament-there is a standing committee of the House-before construction starts.
1 must say, Madam Speaker, that it would be contrary not only to the letter but to the spirit of the law, as well as contrary to the opinion requested and obtained from the law
Privilege-Mr. Knowles
officers of the Crown, for us to proceed in that fashion. My colleague, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), indicated that, as far as his party is concerned, he sees no objection to the order in council and supporting documents being examined by the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments as soon as possible, even next week if need be.
Personally, I do not see why that committee could not meet today, or early next week, to study the order in council of the government. Still, I would hate to see that study delay the start of the pre-build construction. The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, very pertinently, I must say, indicated that the Canadian people, whether it be companies or individuals, have other recourses, which the government does not deny them, and that if anyone should claim that the government has acted illegally, the matter could in various ways be referred to the courts. An injunction could be requested to prevent the start of operations if that upsets the NDP too much.
Be that as it may, there are ways and means of having recourse to the law when people doubt the legality of an order in council, or a government decision or policy. But resorting to a question of privilege because the government has applied section 20(4) of Bill C-25 is splitting hairs, not in four but in eight, 16 or even 32. Basically there is no substance to the question of privilege brought up by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Madam Speaker, I deem it advisable, for the record, to quote a very brief excerpt from the law under which the government has acted: section 20(4) of the act to establish the Northern Pipeline Agency stipulates as follows, and I quote:
The board or the designated officer may rescind, amend or add to the terms and conditions set out in schedule III or deemed to be set out therein but no rescission of or amendment to such a term or condition or addition of a term or condition is effective without the approval of the governor in council.
Madam Speaker, what NDP members and especially their House leader are referring to is an amendment to section 12 of schedule III, something covered by section 20(4) of the act. It cannot be any clearer that the government had the authority through an order in council to do what it did. This time, Madam Speaker, we are not dealing with the legislation of a foreign parliament, a foreign country, or the government of another land. This is legislation of the Canadian Parliament. Hon. members of the House are those who at a given time had to examine it, clause by clause, and when they reached clause 20(4), they realized that in a democratic fashion, following their election by the people, they were giving through a majority mandate to the government the power to do essentially what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is now reproaching it with doing. He is going against the will of Parliament, of a previous parliament, when he questions the right of the government or cabinet to act as it did through an order in council.

July 18, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Knowles
Madam Speaker, it is therefore obvious that there is absolutely no substance to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In my opinion, this is undoubtedly a ploy to air the New Democratic Party's views or its disapproval of the government's policy in this case, but they ought not to use the House's time to pretend that there is in fact substance for a question of privilege and force hon. members to debate a question as to whether, after adopting such an explicit legislation giving the governor in council unequivocal powers, they can take the time of the House to argue that we have now given the governor in council authorization but we wish to go further and have this legislation studied once again in committee.
This is more or less the nature of the request made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I say that it is an abuse of procedures, a traditional means which dates back to the war of 1914 or the last war to which he referred earlier. But this is 1980 and we wish to administer laws in an efficient manner, we have lots of work to do and there is absolutely no legitimate basis for his request.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, even if I endorse the excellent proposal made by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton to ask the Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments to meet as soon as possible in the next days or in the next few weeks, to which we do not object because it would allow members from both sides of the House to make an in-depth study of the order in council, to review our legislative texts, to see to what extent the government application of this Parliament's previously adopted act is carried out democratically, even though I am not opposed to a referral to the appropriate committee, I want to make it clear that in the name of the government I am formally opposed to any reference which might in any way delay the construction of the portion of the pipeline which must be an integral part of the whole project before the end of 1985.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, in concluding, this is what we on this side of the House are submitting: the question is very simple, very clear and what we have done is to respect the legislation adopted by this Parliament. There is absolutely no basis to the question of privilege and I understand that members of the New Democratic Party will have ample time to discuss the motion which will be moved soon to adjourn the House and to express their opinions, just as they have done since the beginning of this week.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:

subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES-NORTHERN PIPELINE ACT-USE OF ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORITY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 think that earlier I made myself clear enough. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES-NORTHERN PIPELINE ACT-USE OF ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORITY

subsubtopic: MR. KNOWLES-NORTHERN PIPELINE ACT-USE OF ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was amazed at the remarks of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) for two reasons. Firstly, it occurred to me that if it is against the spirit of Parliament to refer this matter to the committee, why do we have the committee? Is that not what the committee is for, to examine these matters?
Secondly, and more fundamentally, I would draw to the minister's attention a speech during the debate when the Northern Pipeline Act was passed. We not only have in the House one flip-flop, but now there are two flip-flops. If the minister will examine his speeches, he will see that he comes out quite squarely for the concept of having guarantees that the whole line be built.
Furthermore, the President of the Privy Council comes out along with his predecessor, the Minister of Finance (Mr. July 18, 1980

MacEachen), who had this to say in Hansard for April 4, 1978, at page 4120:
From the very beginning I undertook in the House to ensure that Parliament was brought in at every stage-
Indeed, the government did that. I researched the matter extensively over the last couple of weeks. I looked at all the speeches then and at all the debates in the pipeline committee. I talked to some of the participants, in particular to the Hon. T. C. Douglas who was then a member of this House. I am told by Mr. Douglas that the government then rejected the concept of a pre-build. The concept was brought up and rejected and the act was passed as the Northern Pipeline Act. That was all in the spirit of the act, and hon. members recognize that.
The minister stood up and said that we have the power under section 20, subsection (4). Again, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, that is just an assertion that the government has the power. The minister may be right. I think he is wrong and that it is illegal. I do not see how an apple can be changed into an orange by an order in council, but that may be a matter for the courts.
I appeared at the National Energy Board hearings as an intervener to challenge the power of the board to take this action. There has been a slight misleading, perhaps unintentionally, in the House on this matter. At the hearings, the counsel for the government of Ontario supported my proposition that the board did not really have any jurisdiction in this matter. That was the position of the government of Ontario.
Last night we were told that the government of British Columbia also opposes the pre-build. Perhaps Ontario and British Columbia will bring legal action. I am told that the B.C. Union of Indian Chiefs has also taken that position, and they were at the hearings. Will they bring action? Of course I have, in my status as an intervenor, the right to bring legal action if I so determine. However, the better and ideal remedy would be for the government, as the Minister of Finance said in 1978, to consult the House at all steps and to bring back an amendment to the Northern Pipeline Act. That would be the proper parliamentary procedure, and that is what the government should do if it is really concerned about Parliament. What is the big hurry to go home today? We are paid to be here, and it is our job. We will sit down while the government brings in an amendment. 1. Transport Canada is currently undertaking two studies in the national capital region: one is called Eastern Ontario/Gatineau Area Aviation Development Plan; the other, Ottawa Airport Master Plan.
The first will develop the most appropriate alternative locations and roles for the airports and aeronautical system components for the area; the second will provide a master plan for the development of the Ottawa airport.
Concurrently, a study to develop the passenger terminal complex, including the modification and expansion of the terminal building, associated aircraft parking apron, access roads, public car parking and utilities, to meet the forecasted demand to 1990 design year, has just been completed. The study is being reviewed by Transport Canada headquarters officials.
The passenger terminal complex development is limited to an immediate improvement program which will allow it to meet travel demands up to the year 1990. The long-range development options required to meet the demands beyond this time-frame will be addressed by the airport master plan which is being developed at the present time.
During the airport master plan process, additional studies are being carried out. These will be based on the airport role and airside requirements established as part of the area aviation development plan. The extent of details and costs associated with the additional facilities required to meet the long-range demands cannot be estimated at this time. Order of magnitude costs will be identified when the conceptual alternative airport plans are developed. The order of magnitude cost for the terminal complex development in the pre-design stage is approximately $35 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subsubtopic: FIRST CLASS MAIL STICKERS
speechtext:
1. Yes. Originally these stickers had an "old style" maple leaf with the appropriate text on either side in a symmetrical design. With the introduction of the corporate identity and federal identity programs, these "public use" forms were some of the first redesigned. Design consultants to Canada Post provided an asymmetrical design utilizing the earlier text and the "bar and leaf'. After those stickers were in
use for about a year, Information Canada objected to the irregular use of the "bar and leaf' without the deparmental identification "Canada Post-Postes Canada". A number of prototypes incorporating this additional text were tested but proved to be too complex. Returning to the original "leaf' either centred or in an asymmetrical design was rejected by Information Canada. The only alternative then was to print the stickers without the "bar and leaf' or "leaf'. Printing only the text allowed the sticker to be reduced in size, achieving some economies.
2. It is not the intention of Canada Post to replace the emblem with another indication of the country of origin.

subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON BOARD
speechtext:
1.	(a) What is the function of the Atlantic Salmon Board (b) who are its members (c) how often has the board met?
2.	What recommendations, if any, have been issued by the board?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: ATLANTIC SALMON BOARD
speechtext:
1. (a) Purpose and Objective
As the official focal point for federal-provincial, commercial, recreational and native people consultations relating to resource management, the Atlantic Salmon Board provides to the Federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans advice and recommendations on broad policy matters governing conservation, enhancement and utilization of atlantic salmon as it relates to the five Atlantic provinces.
Duties and Responsibilities
In addition to providing responses to matters specifically referred to the board by the department, the board is expected to consider and provide advice and recommendations on the following:
(i)	Establishment of policy guidelines upon which the department can base decisions on matters pertaining to access to and utilization of the salmon resource, while providing due consideration of such factors as types of fisheries, interception, community impacts, seasonal parameters, markets for salmon products, social and recreational benefits, international implications and developmental or enhancement techniques and strategies; and,

July 18, 1980
Order Paper Questions
(ii)	review of policy options respecting conservation measures and resource management priorities including specification of alternative policy options and assessment of the implications associated with each option.
(b)	The board has representatives of five provincial governments, commercial fishermen, recreational fishermen, native peoples and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. The board is constituted as follows:
-a chairman, appointed by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
-a vice-chairman, appointed by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
-four members representing the department -one representative from each of the five Atlantic region provincial governments -six members representing commercial Atlantic salmon fishing interests
-five members representing Atlantic salmon sports fishing interests
-two members representing native fishermen -one member acting as scientific adviser to the board
(c)	The board has met twice:
(i)	Fredericton: February 13, 1980
(ii)	Quebec City: March 27, 28, 1980
The next meeting is tentatively scheduled for mid-June in Corner Brook, Newfoundland.
2. On February 13, at Fredericton, New Brunswick, three recommendations were issued:
(i)	The Atlantic Salmon Board recommends that compensation to bona fide commercial salmon fishermen be continued during 1980 in order to give the board time to evaluate alternative proposals relating to future commercial Atlantic salmon fisheries.
(ii)	The board recommends that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans prepare initial recommendations to reduce interceptions of Atlantic salmon in distant fisheries for discussion at the next Atlantic Salmon Board meeting.
(iii)	The board recommended that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans encourage his provincial counterparts in Quebec, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia to enter into an Atlantic salmon tagging program comparable to the program that will be initiated in New Brunswick in 1980.
On March 27 and 28, 1980, at Quebec City, P.Q., it was recommended under the following headings:
(a) Terms of Reference It is recommended that:
(i)	the terms of reference as proposed, be amended to ensure that the board report to the hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
(ii)	that the board be free to hold the number of meetings necessary, and that funds be allocated to enable the board to respond to its needs, and that the frequency of board meetings should not be unduly restricted by budgetary or other constraints.
(iii)	that the proposed terms of reference be amended to ensure that reports to the hon. minister be made available to the public on a current basis.
(b)	Interceptions
(i)	to reduce the Newfoundland commercial fishing effort by eliminating all but bona fide fishermen.
(ii)	to standardize the type and quantity of gear used by bona fide fishermen.
(iii)	to licence and control the gear of the cod, mackerel and herring trap fishermen.
(iv)	that the opening of the Newfoundland commercial salmon fishing season be delayed until June 1, or later in coastal areas of Newfoundland where data indicates that such a delay in the opening could help achieve the objective of minimizing the interception of Atlantic salmon of mainland origin.
(c)	Enhancement Task Force
The board recommends the establishment of a Federal-Provincial Atlantic Salmon Board technical team from the five Atlantic provinces to identify the potential for enhancement, identify objectives, coordinate strategy and to report back to the board by October, 1980.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF POLICY RESPECTING DEFENCE CO-OPERATION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence be empowered to hear evidence and consider Canadian policy with respect to future defence co-operation with the United States in the North American region with particular reference to air defence and related arrangements embodied in and flowing from the North American Air Defence Command (NORAD) agreement, and it shall report thereon no later than December 31, 1980.
He said: Madam Speaker, first of all I would like to thank the other parties in the House for their co-operation in allowing this committee to discuss this motion, probably at least during the summer, to prepare for resumption of the session in the fall.

The North American Air Defence Command agreement between Canada and the United States was first concluded in 1958 and then renewed in 1968, 1973 and most recently in 1975 for a five-year period which expired on May 12, 1980. On that date, by means of an exchange of notes, the 1975 agreement was extended for a period of one year. The purpose of the extension is to allow a review by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence of the NORAD agreement and related arrangements as set forth in the accompanying motion.
The agreement provides for the joint North American Air Defence Command through which Canada and the United States co-operate in aerospace surveillance and warning systems and integrated operational control of North American air defence forces, but it does not specify the nature or level of the resources each country should contribute to the common aerospace defence effort. National contributions are determined by each government, often following intensive bilateral consultations.
NORAD operates within the framework of the North Atlantic Treaty, and it has always been perceived by both
countries and by our NATO allies as a symbol of Canada-U.S. co-operation and as a valuable contribution to the over-all security of the NATO area.

At the present time, NORAD has highly effective and economical land, air and space detection and communication systems which can signal the attack of missiles or bombers against North America, prevent unauthorized aircraft from entering the North American airspace, monitor strategic and tactical space operations, and detect the re-entry in the atmosphere of objects from space which represent a hazard for human beings and the environment.

In its deliberations following from today's motion, the SCEAND may wish to examine or receive evidence on the following topics which are relevant to our co-operation with the United States in the Canada-U.S. region of NATO, and in particular to the arrangements flowing from the NORAD agreement: the changing strategic balance and implications for the stability of mutual deterrence; prospects for strategic arms control and the peaceful use of space; the strategic-aerospace threat to North America: past, present and future; strategic-aerospace defences in North America: air defence, passive space defence, active space defence ballistic missile defence; the place of NORAD in strategic defence: recent and planned or potential changes to the organization, roles and force structure of NORAD; Canada's contribution to NORAD; responsibility and cost sharing in NORAD; other elements of Canada-U.S. defence co-operation in the North American region; North American defence co-operation linkages: Canada-U.S. relations generally, defence outside North America, control of civil air traffic, surveillance of space.

1 am sure, Madam Speaker, that in considering those matters and all others they will deem necessary to consider in order to fully understand the agreements on the defence of North America, the committee will be doing something very useful for Parliament and the Canadian people as a whole. The government hopes that the committee will report without delay, so that their recommendations will prepare the ground for the negotiations regarding the ongoing Canada-U.S. cooperation on defence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on this referral. I am particularly pleased that this matter is being opened up for review by members of Parliament, because since taking office the government has shied away from reviews of our country's over-all policy in both foreign affairs and defence. Instead, the government seems to change its policy on a day to day basis. In this week alone we have heard from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) that he favours the increased build-up of a new sophisticated nuclear weapon for use as a deterrent, and then a day later we heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that such is not the case and Canada is as firmly committed to disarmament as it ever was. There seems to be an interesting dynamic in the Liberal caucus, a dynamic that perhaps could best be resolved by a clear, definite policy toward defence in the form of a white paper review.
I should like also to draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that presently my party is undertaking a thorough review of its foreign affairs and defence policies in order to make sure that they are in tune with changing world affairs and events. Circumstances do not remain the same in perpetuity. We in the New Democratic Party realize this and hope that the government, and perhaps the members to our right, would also realize this and not dismiss such reviews as being boring and a lot of needless paperwork.
I believe the traditional reservations of the NDP concerning NORAD are well known to members of the House. We have often in the past questioned the need to defend ourselves against manned bomber attack from the Soviet. In the time it would take such a bomber to reach its targets, the world would have been destroyed four or five times over by intercontinental ballistic missiles. The role of intercepting manned bombers in an age of ICBMs is nearly as useful today as the armour worn by English knights would be as protection against the bullets from a machine gun.
Others have said that the existence of military alliances such as NORAD are contributing factors in heightening world tension. Indeed, recent events where a computer mistaking a goose or a flock of geese for an enemy bomber put North American air defence on red alert and brought the world to the brink of self-annihilation should give us all cause to question how appropriate NORAD is in its present form.
Canada has only limited resources, and we must be careful that they are spent as wisely as possible. We have assigned such a wide array of tasks to our military forces that they are now strained to the limit of their capabilities to cover all bases. Canada is not now and is not likely ever to be a military superpower. There are those in this House who believe that we need all the trappings of a military superpower. A country the size of Canada, with its population accepting all the trappings of a military superpower, is similar to a young boy who dresses up in his father's work clothes. Because he is not big enough, everything hangs strangely and looks out of place. The boy looks like a caricature of the person he is trying to imitate. So

We must take a serious look at our role in world affairs and the contribution we can make with our limited resources. We should not try to be all things to all people, but instead should concentrate our defence efforts in those areas that would best serve our national interest.
The process of reviewing our alliances such as NORAD is a positive one. It gives us the opportunity, at least in this area, to review our present commitment of resources. Mr. Speaker, today is the sixty-fourth day of the first part of the first session of this Thirty-second Parliament and I am delighted to be able to say that during those 64 days we have accomplished more work than we did in the course of both preceding sessions. I shall explain myself, Mr. Speaker. During those 64 days the House of Commons had to face the commitments which had been emphasized very eloquently in the Speech from the Throne. You will remember that the Speech from the Throne stated, and I quote:
Canadians expect much of this Parliament. The country asks for action and action now. The first task is to clear the accumulation of essential legislation left from previous Parliaments. This backlog must be dispatched expeditiously so
that the affairs of the state may be put in good order. To that end, my government is relying on the good will of members and senators of all parties.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to say publicly that indeed the wish expressed by the Governor General in the Speech from the Throne has been fulfilled thanks to parliamentary spirit and co-operation of all members on both sides of the House. Of course, some would have liked to see additional legislation or measures other than those which were introduced to be debated and passed. However, in our responsibility as government we had to take into account the fact that the country had held two elections within a year and that Parliament having failed to sit without interruption, there was an accumulation of legislation. There was disorder in the House in the sense that it was absolutely essential and urgent to pass at least 15 bills which had acquired a technical urgency.
As an example, and to quote only a few of them, it was urgent to adopt Bill C-2 to amend the Immigration Act. It was equally urgent to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Employment Tax Credit Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act. All these measures, Mr. Speaker, were necessary to meet the needs of the people and of various classes of society, so that people could benefit from funds made available to certain categories by virtue of some acts which were expiring. So, at first we were facing that accumulation of legislative measures resulting from two elections, and it was our responsibility as a government and it was the responsibility of all of us as parliamentarians to try in the first few weeks, in the first few months, to prevent this new Parliament from making mistakes, to help it be responsible and to pass those pieces of legislation after reasonable debate. This is what happened.
I am pleased to confirm and to report what most of my colleagues know by now, namely, that since April 15 the House has permitted royal assent to be given to 25 bills instead of the 15 mentioned. Among those bills are not only those which were technically urgent but some which enabled the government to implement the most important electoral commitment they made, namely, to increase the guaranteed income supplement for older citizens. We succeeded through all those accumulated pieces of legislation, with the co-operation of all parties, to pass that bill which raises the guaranteed income supplement of our senior citizens, of those who are least able to protect themselves against inflation and the economic problems countries such as ours are experiencing. We have also succeeded in the present constitutional context, besides more technically urgent legislation, in securing the contribution of all parties to adopt "O Canada" expeditiously, after all those years, as the national anthem of a country we all want to be united and stronger.
And, Mr. Speaker, we have also been able to rearrange the parliamentary schedule of supply business. If I were asked as government House leader to point to the most important
July 18, 1980

measure, policy or agreement during this first session, I would not hesitate at all to indicate the major agreement concluded about supply business. My colleagues the House leaders of the other two parties will agree that the most complex procedure in our rules is that of supply.
Because there have been two elections in one year, not only had estimates for last year not been approved by Parliament but those for the current year could not be approved either, outside a time frame like that which is normally provided for under our Standing Orders. To put it another way, because the estimates for the current year had not been tabled in due course on account of the date the election had been called and the date Parliament had reconvened, none of the provisions of the many sections and paragraphs of our Standing Orders dealing with time limits and fixed dates for the adoption of supply bills, and none of the provisions providing for natural, legal and time honoured cutoff dates could apply, due again to the fact that the election had been held on a certain date and that the main estimates had not been tabled at the proper time.
Parliament was therefore in a very confused state. Theoretically, the opposition parties could have taken this opportunity to debate endlessly any item of the estimates, under any department, without any time limit. Parliament could have sat for weeks and months, without any control other than that provided for under Standing Order 33, which is not the most popular section on Parliament Hill, namely, that the government has the authority to use closure to put an end without notice to any debate in the House, thereby preventing members of the opposition from expressing their views as fully as they would care to.
So fortunately we did not have to use Standing Order 33. The opposition parties through their parliamentary leaders, after lengthy but harmonious discussions, made it possible to reach in due time that major agreement I referred to earlier. I say it is a major agreement because we were in a situation where there was absolutely no order possible in this House on the business of the House unless we used the real guillotine which would have created a commotion, poisoned the climate and compromised seriously, 1 have no hesitation to say, the passage of other bills which had become urgent. What made that major agreement possible and was making it even more important is the fact that we needed interim supplies by May 15 when the Governor General's warrants allowing the government to spend and administer expired.
There again, the agreement was all the more crucial as it had to be reached in the month following the opening of the session, that is before May 15, and we were limited by time and the understandable psychological predispositions of opposition members, following the change in government, but despite all those obstacles, those time limitations, that psychological stress, the parliamentary spirit prevailed-and I have no hesitation to say so-and the parliamentary leaders came to

an agreement which deserves to be pointed out and which made it possible not only to put order in the business of supply, but we were able to set a very orderly parliamentary timetable to work in a reasonable and to a certain extent innovative way. Indeed the House will have to sit for six days in Committee of the Whole this fall to consider estimates but not only was some order put in the business of supply but at the same time allowed the climate to remain favourable to doing legislative work and, as I mentioned earlier, the passage of 25 pieces of legislation that were absolutely essential for most of them and the others will allow the House to be free this fall to dispose of other measures such as the ones we introduced yesterday, namely, the access to information bill, the bill to turn the Post Office into a Crown corporation, and many other economic and social measures to come.
So, Mr. Speaker, I put my finger on what 1 consider to be the major development in that first session. Even if there is agreement on the business of supply, that is no excitement for the public. Even if there is nothing glaring about that agreement, it is not a scandal, it is not a sensational measure but a parliamentary measure that is basically essential, crucial, not only to draw up our schedule so that we can dispose of the business of supply, but also to develop a spirit of co-operation, a true parliamentary spirit such as we have known in the last weeks.
As concerns the achievements made in this first stage of the first session, I referred to the 25 bills that have been passed, I referred to the parliamentary schedule for the business of supply. There is also our experiment with parliamentary task forces that my knowledgeable colleague from Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker) likes to call, quite rightly, special committees of the House of Commons. And the House knows that they are actually parliamentary task forces consisting of a smaller number of members. There are six now at work in six different fields of public interest and they are instructed to act rapidly and report to this House within a limited period of time, by December 19, and they may help us to find out how we can make full use of the talents of all hon. members from every region of the country, and more particularly from western Canada.
I think the conclusion of this agreement for the setting up of parliamentary task forces in the course of the first part of the session is an event which deserves to be underlined because it was the result of co-operation between all parties in this House. We must stress that the climate in which we worked has been unusual. Several of us have worked twice as hard, Mr. Speaker, as we were actively involved in a campaign of major importance for the future of our country and I am talking of course of the referendum campaign in Quebec. The first part of the session ran parallel with the pre-referendum campaign and the referendum campaign itself and a very large number of hon. members representing all areas of Canada

July 18, 1980
Summer Recess
have directly or indirectly helped bring about the wanted results of the Quebec referendum either by way of their personal and direct involvement in the field or by way of their attitude here in the House or by way of the very nature of their contributions in this place or by way of the things they did or refrained from doing. I take this opportunity to stress the merit which the parliamentarians of this House deserve for having contributed to our victory in the Quebec referendum.
We had the twofold responsibility of putting our country's affairs in order, at least with regard to the backlog of procedures and legislations. We had the twofold responsibility governing the country on the one hand and on the other being involved in a crucial campaign in order to secure Canada's unity and this country's survival. I think that on both sides of the House we have all taken our responsibilities to heart, and we did make the necessary effort which was met with the success we all know and which is a credit to all parliamentarians. But I would be remiss if 1 did not emphasize the tremendous work done by the very great majority of the hon. members for the province of Quebec in that respect.
Then, when we consider the volume of business 1 just summarized, this first part of the session may not appear to be sensational for certain people. They would say that Parliament did some business but it was dull. For sure, there has been nothing outstanding, there has been no scandal nor perhaps the kind of debates we have seen when the Canadian flag was adopted. However, there is a fact we all must admit, and it is that during its first two months of existence this Parliament has been very efficient. This government has behaved responsibly. This has to be said of Parliament also, not just of the government. And when I say that Parliament has behaved responsibly, this implies that members on both sides of the House who of course do not always agree with what we are doing, who have criticized some of our bills but have never abused their right to criticize, considering that the country had been through two elections and that it was urgent to dispose of some business to which I referred earlier.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to convey my special thanks not only to members of this House but also to the senators, Madam Speaker, her assistants, the officers at the table and all the officials of the House of Commons as well as the pages who have all been very efficient and quite devoted and who at this time of the year, either on account of their children, their parents, their families, their spouses feel the need to withdraw and lead a normal life, whether they be members, employees of the House of Commons, members of the Press Gallery, the media or the public, most of whom are already on holidays or are going to be soon.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank all those people who helped make Parliament during this first stage of the first session so productive and responsible and 1 am sure that all my colleagues on this side of the House will join me in extending to
all those who deserve them and whom I have just mentioned my very special thanks.
Finally, I wish to deal with one question but I see that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is absent-no, he is here. I am addressing my remarks especially to his party through him who knows the parliamentary spirit which induced us to co-operate as parliamentary leaders during this session and this comment, of course, is also aimed at the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton.
He knows the extent to which there has never been any desire on this side of the House, neither, I believe, on the Conservative side, but my colleague will speak on their behalf, will be tricky. Admittedly, it would be hard to fool the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre where procedure is concerned, in view of his long experience and wide knowledge of the rules. However, we have always refrained from attempting to take advantage of hon. members by resorting to procedural games, and as House leader it has always been my policy to use an open and straightforward approach, which up till now has been producing results. 1 would like to tell him this afternoon with the same open and straightforward frame of mind, that I am fully aware, after hearing the statements made up to this point by his leader, for whom I have much respect, by himself or by other hon. members, that he is looking for a way to tell the public at large, for reasons known to his party, his opposition to a government policy very well known to him.
The adjournment motion is a means by which his fellow members can make their points. One of many means, because up to this point, this week at least, during the question period, on the eighth day of the throne speech debate yesterday, following the statement made by the minister yesterday evening until 11.30 p.m., when every contribution had been made and nobody asked to be recognized, and today again, at least until four o'clock and later if his party so desires, he can have all the time required to fully express his views.
Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
So what I would like to tell the hon. member and his colleagues, and the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), is that there is no rule we could apply to prevent the New Democratic Party from requiring the hon. members on both sides of the House, the staff employees of the House and all those who are interested in our debates, either the media or the public, to come back next Monday, if such is the wish of the New Democratic Party. Clearly then, there is no authority whatsoever in our rules under which I, as House leader, or any member here could force the hon. members to adjourn today. In other words, if NDP members want to return next Monday at all costs, nobody can prevent them. That is quite clear and 1 am aware of it. However, there are rules which allow members to sit beyond the regular sitting
July 18, 1980

hours. Today is Friday. It is the last day of the week and usually the House does not sit on Friday evening. I for one, and I speak only for my party because I do not wish to involve the Progressive Conservative Party, believe I speak for all my colleagues on this side when I offer, if NDP members deem it necessary, to extend the sitting hours indefinitely today so as to allow all members who want to speak today to do so. My learned colleague, the House leader for the New Democratic Party, is well aware that any matter of government policy may be dealt with on the adjournment motion. NDP members may take advantage of that motion to speak on any other subject, either on the veterans' pensions we willingly granted a short time ago with the co-operation of all parties, or on the Alaska pipeline or on the $35 paid to pensioners by the Liberal government. I repeat that we are prepared to allow NDP members to sit indefinitely today until they have fully made their point on one or several government policies. Once again, they are free to accept or reject our proposal, that is their political judgment. We, as members of Parliament, shall have no choice but to return next Monday, if such is the wish of NDP members.
So, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to reiterate my thanks to all those who deserve them, and remind the House of the parliamentary spirit that has prevailed until now, banking of course on that of the New Democratic Party, so that we can, in orderly fashion, without abuse and humanely, discuss fully a matter of interest to them, without in any way penalizing unduly people who do not share their views, all the more so when their objections concern measures that have been passed according to parliamentary rules and an act passed by this Parliament.
So, once again, Mr. Speaker, in closing I express the wish that, with regard to the future, hon. members of all parties will take advantage of the summer break, whether it starts today or next week, to reflect seriously on what amendments could be made to some of our rules with a view to ultimately making this Parliament, while respecting its spirit, of course, more efficient, more modern and also more humane.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before beginning my remarks on this motion may I take the opportunity while I am on my feet to correct what might have been a misimpression flowing from remarks I made on a procedural matter earlier this day. I was commenting on the fact that I did not at that moment have in my hands copies of Hansard. I would not want that to be interpreted as a criticism of the Hansard staff. As the House well knows, we sat exceptionally long hours last night, and if there is fault to be assigned for Hansard not being ready for the 11 a.m. session, it is with those of us who speak, rather than with the reporters who record the proceedings of this House.

Hear, hear!
Summer Recess

Let me make some beginning remarks in response to the observations of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). I think that he will allow me, and that the House will agree, to congratulate him on a very graceful act of self-congratulations for the manner in which matters have been proceeding through the House. I will have a little more to say on that in just a moment.
Before doing that, however, Mr. Speaker, I want to turn to the proposition that he has made to the New Democratic Party regarding the possibility of this House not seeing the clock tonight and allowing members of Parliament who want to speak on the adjournment debate to have an exceptionally long Friday. Certainly, on behalf of my colleagues in the official opposition, I can say that arrangement would be acceptable to us. We would agree to a procedure of that kind if it were to be proposed and necessary.
Hear, hear!

Let me deal now with some of the matters that the President of the Privy Council, the House leader of the government, raised. He talked about the legislation that has been brought forward. I will say on his behalf that he had the good grace to admit that most of the legislation was proposed and prepared by governments other than his own. He admitted that indeed what this government has done, primarily, in this first session of a majority Parliament, when the nation faces urgent issues, is deal with housekeeping matters, with matters that were already prepared, with matters that would have been brought forward in any event. There has been very little indication of any new initiatives by this government.
I must say in passing that I noted with a certain humour that the President of the Privy Council took credit for the special committees of Parliament looking into matters which are of interest to members of this House. He well knows, and members well know, and students of the parliamentary process should know, that what this government tried to do was run around the rules of Parliament by establishing task forces that will report to ministers and not to Parliament. It was only after pressure from this side of the House, and this party in particular, that the government followed the rules and practices to respect the privileges of the House of Commons. Instead of having task forces which answer to ministers and could then be forgotten, the government reverted to establishment of special committees of the House of Commons which will report to the House and whose recommendations will be debatable by the whole House under the eyes of the country.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!
I hear the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) who speaks much more often and much more eloquently from his seat than on his feet-

Hear, hear!

speechtext: Order, please. I say again that the hon. member for Regina West is entering into debate. I would ask him to be so kind as to co-operate with the usual procedure of the House and permit the right hon. Leader of the Opposition to continue.

Mr. Speaker, I was not distorting the position of the hon. member. I was simply reviewing it and recalling it to his mind. I am not at all surprised that he is unhappy when that is done. He would also be unhappy were I to recall to his mind the positions, in the plural, of his party on NATO, the positions, in the plural, of his party on NORAD, and the positions, in the plural, and the contradiction of his party on the Quebec referendum. We could do that, but I do not intend to spend very much time reminding the New Democratic Party of the inconsistencies that have become a way of life with them.
Hear, hear!

What I wanted to deal with instead was some of the records of the government and indeed, in my opening remarks, some of the matters that were prepared and ready to be introduced by the government I had the honour to lead. For some peculiar reason those things have disappeared and have not made their way to the legislative agenda of this House. 1 think, for example, of the beef import law which was ready for introduction last year and of which nothing has been seen. In light of the references of the President of the Privy Council to his interest in parliamentary reform, 1 think of the very comprehensive package of parliamentary reforms that had as a purpose not the convenience of the government but the powers, the rights and the respect of individual members of Parliament. That package was introduced by our government, but nothing has been seen of it.
I think, for example, of the proposal we made to have an open, public inquiry, into all aspects of nuclear energy in this country, instead of a silent, quiet, private, hidden inquiry by officials of the Government of Canada who have the most to hide. We believed in openness. We acted on openness, and they have acted in the exact opposite direction. Or we could have spoken about the committee on voluntarism designed to try to have the Parliament of Canada recognize the great damage that is being done to the spirit of Canadians by the growth of bureaucracy, both public and private, to have the Parliament of Canada address directly the problems and the potential of encouraging more individuals through voluntary organizations to play a larger role themselves in the development and in the improvement of our Canadian society. That was a parliamentary special committee proposed by the government of which I had the honour to be leader, a parliamentary committee on a
July 18, 1980

matter which apparently is of no interest to the government now in office.
There is a long list again. I am reminded of the report of the public accounts committee today. The Conservative government established a special committee to look into the very serious problem of cost overruns. That was a committee which would have allowed full public discussion of that important public question which this government has abandoned. It has ditched that idea. I note with interest the unanimous report of the public accounts committee of this House of Commons which was brought down today. It recommended again explicitly that the committee on cost overruns which we established, which this government abandoned, should be established again and established immediately. Certainly that is a view which this whole party supports, as well as being the unanimous position of the public accounts committee of the House of Commons.

Hear, hear!
